extracted.intended_audience: business school instructors and students (public relations / crisis communication), corporate communications practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: A teaching case analyzing United Airlines Flight 3411 and the company's public communications during the crisis; useful for evaluating crisis-response statements, channels, tone, and remedial actions. Focuses on real-world examples of what worsened and what remedial steps were taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of response
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond quickly to rapidly spreading news and social media; initial delays or poorly timed statements can exacerbate backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News regarding the Flight 3411 incident "spread rapidly throughout social media sites and mainstream media." United released a first public statement midday April 10 and further communications that evening and the following days. The case notes shares "fell 6.3% in pre-market trading" the next day, showing how rapid public reaction and market impact follow viral content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of empathy and sincere apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications should convey genuine empathy and heartfelt apology; weak or formulaic apologies are criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Munoz’s first statement — "This is an upsetting event to all of us here at United. I apologize for having to re-accommodate these customers." — was "publicly criticized for lack of sensations, empathy, and feelings." Later stronger wording included: "my deepest apologies for what happened... I take full responsibility." Use language that centers the harmed party and expresses sincere remorse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid victim‑blaming language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid language that blames or characterizes the harmed party in ways that appear defensive or dismissive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Munoz’s leaked employee email summarized the passenger as "disruptive and belligerent," which the public described as "offensive and insensitive." The case shows such descriptions inflame backlash; communications should avoid blaming the victim and instead focus on facts and remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take responsibility and own the mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: Public leaders should accept responsibility rather than defensiveness; acknowledging fault can de-escalate public anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After backlash Munoz "decided to change course and take full responsibility," issuing a statement: "we take full responsibility and we will work to make it right." This shift coincided with attempts to repair reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide concrete corrective actions and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Announce specific remedial measures and timelines for review/implementation to demonstrate commitment to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: United promised a thorough review and committed to "communicate the results of our review by April 30th." Public commitments included not asking law enforcement to remove passengers except for safety, reviewing crew movement policies, and improving training programs. Specific deadlines and named actions increase credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between internal and external messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure internal communications are aligned with public statements; leaks or contradictory internal messages worsen crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An emailed internal message that defended employees was leaked and contradicted public-facing apologies, worsening backlash. The case highlights that a separate internal tone that blames victims or defends actions can undermine external reputation management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate channels and maintain a central information hub
rubrics_metrics.description: Designate and use official channels (company blog/newsroom, social media, press conferences) as primary sources for updates to control the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: United relied on its weblog, UNITED HUB, as the main information source and used Facebook and Twitter for initial responses. The case also references a press conference and Congressional testimony as communication channels. Centralized, authoritative channels help manage information flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and timely follow‑up reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate follow-up findings and outcomes of reviews; keep stakeholders informed about what was found and what was changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Munoz committed to communicate the results of the review by a specific date. The case documents subsequent policy changes (e.g., new policy to prevent last-minute boarding for crew members) and mentions reaching an undisclosed settlement with the passenger — highlighting the value of reporting concrete outcomes where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement policy and training reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Announce and carry out operational policy changes and training improvements to address root causes and prevent recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: United announced concrete changes: it "will not ask law enforcement officers to remove passengers from our flights unless it is a matter of safety and security," it started a review of crew movement and incentivizing volunteers, and pledged to "fully review and improve our training programs to ensure our employees are prepared and empowered to put our customers first." Such substantive reforms support credibility beyond words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor tone and content to audience (public vs employees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust messaging to suit the audience (employees, customers, regulators, investors) while maintaining core consistency; avoid contradictory emphases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Munoz issued different statements: one to the public and one email to employees (later leaked). The employee email defended staff and recapped preliminary reports, while public statements shifted toward apology and responsibility. The leakage showed how differing tones can cause problems—audience‑specific messaging should still align on core facts and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor social media and be prepared for viral evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively monitor social media for emerging content (videos, posts) and prepare rapid, evidence‑aware responses when viral material appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The incident was triggered and amplified by passenger-shot videos distributed on social platforms (Twitter/X, Facebook). Public reaction included cutting loyalty cards and celebrity commentary. The case implies the need to watch and respond to social channels because they drive public perception and can escalate issues quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational remediation (apology + outreach + restitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine public apology with direct outreach to affected individuals and, where appropriate, compensation/settlement and policy change to restore trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: United CEO and the company called Dr. Dao to offer apologies and later reached an undisclosed settlement; they implemented policy changes (no last‑minute boarding for crew) and publicized commitments. The case shows that apology alone may be insufficient without direct redress and demonstrable change.
